objectives: Understand Nakamoto consensus + PoW + chain quality.
Operate modern cloud + microservices + service mesh.

slides.title: Byzantine consensus: PBFT, Tendermint, HotStuff, Diem/Aptos/Sui
slides.body:
**Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT)**: consensus when nodes may behave arbitrarily — crash, lie, equivocate, collude. Lamport, Shostak, Pease (1982 TOPLAS 'The Byzantine Generals Problem') proved synchronous BFT needs **N ≥ 3f + 1** to tolerate f Byzantine faults; with signatures + partial synchrony the same bound (Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer 1988).

**PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance)** (Miguel Castro + Barbara Liskov 1999 OSDI, 'Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance'): the first BFT protocol fast enough for real systems (low latency + only constant slowdown over crash-only). Pattern:
- **Primary** broadcasts a `pre-prepare` with sequence number.
- All replicas multicast `prepare` messages; when 2f+1 prepares match, the proposal is **prepared**.
- All replicas multicast `commit`; when 2f+1 commits match, the proposal is **committed**.
- **View change** if the primary fails or equivocates.
- Quadratic O(N²) message complexity in normal operation.

PBFT inspired a generation of Byzantine protocols. Castro + Liskov went on to influence cloud + DB design; Liskov also won the Turing Award (2008).

**Tendermint** (Buchman + Kwon 2014-, Cosmos SDK): adapts PBFT to public blockchains. Round-based; deterministic finality (no probabilistic chain). Validators rotate proposers; weighted by stake. Used by Cosmos Hub, Binance Chain, Terra. Spawned the **ABCI (Application Blockchain Interface)** abstraction separating consensus from application state.

**HotStuff** (Maofan Yin et al. 2019 PODC, 'HotStuff: BFT Consensus with Linearity and Responsiveness'): breakthrough Byzantine protocol. Key innovations:
- **Linear communication complexity** O(N) per view (vs PBFT's O(N²)) via threshold signatures + leader-driven communication.
- **Pipelined 3-chain commit**: a block is committed when it has a 3-chain of QCs (Quorum Certificates) above it; equivalent to PBFT's prepare + pre-commit + commit phases pipelined.
- **Optimistic responsiveness**: progress at network speed when leader honest, regardless of timeouts.
- **Simple view-change**: just bump view number; no special protocol.
- Foundation of modern BFT blockchains.

**Diem (Libra) → Aptos + Sui** (the lineage):
- **Diem/Libra** (Meta 2019-2022, paused): permissioned BFT blockchain; used **DiemBFT** (HotStuff variant). Introduced the **Move language** (Sam Blackshear et al.) — resource-oriented, statically typed, designed for digital assets.
- **Aptos** (Aptos Labs 2022, ex-Diem team): **AptosBFT** (HotStuff successor with optimistic ordering + parallel execution via Block-STM); uses Move; high throughput.
- **Sui** (Mysten Labs 2022, ex-Diem team): **Narwhal + Bullshark** (DAG-based consensus); objects vs accounts; parallel execution by default; Move-based.
- Both target ~100k-500k TPS via parallelism + DAG mempools.

**Other Byzantine systems**:
- **Algorand** (Micali 2017): VRF-based committee selection + Byzantine agreement; no leader; finalizes in seconds.
- **Avalanche** (Rocket et al. 2018): metastable consensus via random subsampling + repeated queries; subsecond finality.
- **Solana**: Tower BFT (variant on PBFT with proof-of-history clocks) + leader pipelining.
- **Ethereum 2.0 / Casper FFG + LMD-GHOST**: hybrid finality gadget over a longest-chain fork-choice.

**Practical lessons from BFT research**:
- 3f+1 is fundamental; only signatures + partial synchrony preserve it.
- Quadratic vs linear complexity matters for >100 validators.
- Pipelining + threshold signatures unlock throughput.
- DAG-based mempools (Narwhal, DAG-Rider, Aleph) decouple data dissemination from consensus.
- Move offers safer asset semantics than EVM Solidity.

slides.title: Nakamoto consensus: Bitcoin, PoW, longest chain, chain quality, selfish mining
slides.body:
**Bitcoin** (Satoshi Nakamoto 2008, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', anonymous whitepaper; first block Jan 2009). Achieves Byzantine agreement among an open + permissionless set of validators with **Nakamoto consensus**:

**Proof-of-Work (PoW)** (Dwork-Naor 1992 'Pricing via Processing or Combatting Junk Mail'; Hashcash by Adam Back 1997): finding a nonce such that H(block_header) < target is computationally expensive but verification is cheap. Difficulty adjusts so blocks come ~every 10 min. Miners compete; the first to find a valid block broadcasts; others build on it.

**Longest-chain rule (heaviest-chain in PoW work)**: honest nodes always follow the chain with the most accumulated work. A reorg replaces a shorter prefix when a heavier alternative emerges.

**Nakamoto consensus properties** (Garay, Kiayias, Leonardos 2015 'The Bitcoin Backbone Protocol'):
- **Common prefix**: with overwhelming probability the prefixes of any two honest nodes' chains agree after a security parameter k blocks.
- **Chain quality**: an upper bound on the fraction of blocks contributed by the adversary; with f < 1/2 hashrate, eventually >50% of blocks are honest.
- **Chain growth**: chains grow at a predictable rate.
- Probabilistic finality — no deterministic 'committed' point; convention: 6 confirmations ≈ secure.

**51% attack**: adversary with >50% hashrate can rewrite arbitrary history + double-spend. Bitcoin's economic security depends on the cost of acquiring + operating that hashrate.

**Selfish mining (Eyal-Sirer 2014, FC)**: a miner with >25% hashrate can profitably withhold blocks + release strategically, gaining more than fair share. Mitigations: uniform tie-breaking, FruitChains (Pass-Shi 2016), publishing fast.

**Variants + alternatives**:
- **Ethereum 1.0** (Buterin 2013-2022): PoW + smart contracts; **EVM** + Solidity. Transitioned to **PoS** in 'The Merge' (Sept 2022) via Casper FFG + LMD-GHOST.
- **Proof-of-Stake (PoS)**: validators stake currency; selected to propose by stake weight; misbehavior slashed. Lower energy + native finality (e.g., Ethereum: ~13 min full finality).
- **Proof-of-History (Solana)**: cryptographic verifiable delay function (VDF) ordering.
- **Proof-of-Space (Chia)**: plot disk space instead of compute.
- **PoW alternatives** (Equihash, RandomX, scrypt): ASIC resistance attempts.

**Trilemma** (Buterin's blockchain trilemma): security + decentralization + scalability — pick two. PoW Bitcoin chose security + decentralization. Scaling research (rollups, sharding, DAGs) attempts the third leg.

**Layer 2 + rollups**:
- **Optimistic rollups** (Optimism, Arbitrum): assume valid, allow fraud proofs.
- **ZK rollups** (zkSync, Starknet, Polygon zkEVM): cryptographic validity proofs (SNARKs/STARKs).
- **Validium**, **data availability layers** (Celestia, EigenDA).

**Comparison with classical BFT**:
- BFT (PBFT, Tendermint, HotStuff): permissioned, fast finality, scales to ~100s of validators.
- Nakamoto: permissionless, probabilistic finality, scales to thousands of miners but throughput-limited.
- Modern PoS chains (Aptos, Sui, Solana, Cosmos) attempt to combine: permissionless + classical-BFT-style finality via stake-weighted committees.

**MEV (Maximal Extractable Value)** (Daian et al. 2019 'Flash Boys 2.0'): block producers can reorder/insert/censor transactions for profit. Has reshaped blockchain economic security; led to MEV-Boost + proposer-builder separation in Ethereum.

**Energy debate**: Bitcoin PoW ~150 TWh/yr (Cambridge index); comparable to medium country. Driver of PoS migrations + ESG critiques.

slides.title: Modern cloud + microservices + service mesh + WASM edge
slides.body:
**Modern distributed systems** live on cloud-native infrastructure. The dominant patterns of the 2020s:

**Microservices** (Lewis + Fowler 2014, after Amazon's 'two-pizza teams' + Netflix): small, independently deployable services communicating via APIs/events. Trade monolithic complexity for distributed-systems complexity. Best when team autonomy + scaling axes are clearly separable.

**Containers + Kubernetes**:
- **Docker** (2013): standardized container packaging.
- **Kubernetes (k8s)** (Google → CNCF 2014): container orchestration; descended from Borg (Verma et al. 2015, EuroSys) + Omega (Schwarzkopf et al.). Concepts: pod (group of containers), deployment, service, ingress, statefulset, daemonset, CRDs. **Operator pattern** (CoreOS 2016) automates application lifecycle.
- **Etcd** (CoreOS, now CNCF): Raft-based KV store — Kubernetes's control-plane database.
- **CRI/CNI/CSI**: pluggable runtime + network + storage interfaces.

**Service mesh**: layer-7 cross-cutting concerns (mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, traffic shifting, observability) handled by sidecar proxies — out of application code.
- **Istio** (Google + IBM 2017): Envoy-based; rich policy engine; arguably heavy.
- **Linkerd** (Buoyant; CNCF): Rust-based; minimal; lower overhead.
- **Consul Connect** (HashiCorp): mesh on Consul.
- **Cilium Service Mesh** (Isovalent → Cisco): eBPF-based, sidecar-less in many cases; performance gains.
- **Envoy** (Lyft, Matt Klein 2016): the dominant L7 proxy underpinning Istio + many mesh + API gateway products.

**Distributed tracing + observability** (Dapper paper, Sigelman et al. 2010): trace IDs propagate across services + spans capture timing. **OpenTelemetry** (CNCF) is the unifying standard. Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, Honeycomb, Lightstep, Tempo. Logs + metrics + traces = three pillars; **wide events** (Charity Majors) increasingly preferred over metric-only.

**Serverless**:
- **AWS Lambda** (2014), **Cloud Functions**, **Azure Functions**: per-request billing, automatic scaling.
- **Cold-start problem**: container init for languages like Java + .NET takes hundreds of ms; mitigated by SnapStart, provisioned concurrency, warm pools.
- **Faster runtimes** (Go, Rust, Node, Python with snapshot) reduce cold-starts to ~50 ms.
- **Firecracker** (AWS 2018): microVM for Lambda + Fargate; sub-second cold start.

**Edge compute + WASM**:
- **Cloudflare Workers** (2017): V8 isolates instead of containers; sub-ms cold start; runs at ~300+ edge POPs.
- **WebAssembly (WASM)** (2017+): portable bytecode initially for browsers, now server-side (Wasmtime, Wasmer, WasmEdge). WASI standardizes system access. Smaller + faster than containers; sandboxed by default.
- **Fly.io**: Firecracker microVMs at edge; deploy Docker apps to regions globally.
- **Deno Deploy**, **Vercel Edge Functions**, **Fastly Compute@Edge** (WASM-based) — converging stack.

**Modern data + ML infra**:
- **Vector databases** (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, pgvector) for retrieval-augmented generation.
- **Lakehouse** (Databricks 2020): Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi over object storage.
- **Feature stores** (Tecton, Feast) for ML feature consistency.
- **MLOps** + model serving: Triton, Ray Serve, vLLM, Anyscale.

**Geographic + latency-aware design**:
- **Anycast**: BGP-routed nearest POP.
- **Multi-region active-active**: NewSQL or eventually-consistent stores.
- **CDN + edge caching**: Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai.
- **5G + MEC**: mobile edge compute for latency-critical apps.

**Reliability practices**:
- **SRE** (Site Reliability Engineering, Google 2003+; Beyer et al. book 2016): error budgets, SLO/SLI/SLA.
- **Chaos engineering** (Netflix Chaos Monkey, Gremlin): inject failures in production.
- **Progressive delivery**: feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Statsig), canary, blue-green.
- **Observability-driven development**: instrument first, ship, observe.
- **Capacity planning + load testing**: Vegeta, k6, Locust.

**Open-source ecosystem in 2026**: Kubernetes is the standard runtime; eBPF-based networking (Cilium) is ascendant; service mesh is consolidating around Istio + Linkerd + Cilium; observability is OpenTelemetry-everywhere; WASM at the edge replaces some serverless containers; NewSQL (CockroachDB, Yugabyte, Spanner) for transactional cores; Kafka + Flink for streaming. The pieces compose into resilient, globally-distributed, observable systems — the legacy of every paper from Lamport (1978) onward.

question.question: Pick consensus for three scenarios: private consortium, public blockchain, internal Kubernetes
question.goal: Three deployments: (A) 7-bank consortium ledger; (B) public permissionless token chain; (C) internal Kubernetes etcd cluster. Choose consensus + justify.

acceptedAnswers: permissioned BFT — PBFT or HotStuff-style (Tendermint, Diem/AptosBFT); tolerate up to 2 Byzantine of 7

steps.reveal: **Permissioned BFT** — PBFT (Castro-Liskov 1999) or HotStuff (Yin et al. 2019). With N=7 + 3f+1 bound, you tolerate f=2 Byzantine banks. Deterministic finality is critical for legal/regulatory clarity. Tendermint (Cosmos) or Hyperledger Fabric + Quorum/Besu commonly chosen. Lower latency than PoW + no energy cost.

acceptedAnswers: Nakamoto consensus (PoW) or PoS BFT (Ethereum 2.0, Aptos, Sui, Solana, Cosmos)

steps.reveal: **Nakamoto consensus** (Bitcoin-style PoW) or **PoS BFT** like Ethereum 2.0 (Casper + LMD-GHOST), Aptos (HotStuff-derived), Sui (Narwhal + Bullshark), Solana (Tower BFT + PoH), Cosmos (Tendermint). For 2026 the energy + finality story strongly favors PoS BFT. Choose by ecosystem (smart-contract VM: EVM vs Move vs Solana SVM), throughput target, decentralization vs throughput tradeoff (Buterin's trilemma).

acceptedAnswers: Raft (crash-only consensus, 2f+1 nodes); etcd uses etcd-raft

steps.reveal: **Raft** (Ongaro + Ousterhout 2014). Etcd uses **etcd-raft** library. Nodes are trusted (not Byzantine). Typical deployments: 3 (tolerate 1) or 5 (tolerate 2). Strong consistency + leader-based replication; fast in healthy operation. Kubernetes API server uses etcd for control-plane state — every Kubernetes deployment in the world relies on Raft.

steps.prompt: Why is BFT overkill for case (C)?

acceptedAnswers: BFT needs 3f+1 instead of 2f+1 + extra rounds + signatures; only worth it under adversarial threat

steps.reveal: BFT (PBFT/HotStuff) needs **3f+1** nodes, **3 phases** (pre-prepare, prepare, commit), + signatures or HMACs on every message. The cost is justified only when nodes can be adversarial (compromised, byzantine). Inside a trusted datacenter + with crash-only failures, Raft's 2f+1 + 1 phase is cheaper + simpler. Use BFT when you cannot trust the operators; otherwise Raft is the right tool.

question.question: What's the breakthrough in HotStuff (Yin et al. 2019) compared to PBFT?
options: **HotStuff** (Yin, Malkhi, Reiter, Gueta, Abraham 2019 PODC) achieves **linear O(N) communication complexity** per view via **threshold signatures + leader-driven broadcasts**, vs PBFT's **quadratic O(N²)**. It also introduces a **pipelined 3-chain commit** — a block is committed when there is a 3-chain of Quorum Certificates above it; functionally equivalent to PBFT's prepare + pre-commit + commit phases but pipelined for throughput. Plus **optimistic responsiveness** (progress at network speed when leader honest, regardless of timeouts) + simple view-change (just bump view number). These make HotStuff the foundation of modern BFT blockchains: Diem/Libra's DiemBFT, Aptos's AptosBFT, parts of Cosmos's ABCI++. PBFT (Castro-Liskov 1999) was the first practical BFT but did not scale beyond ~30 validators; HotStuff scales to hundreds.
question.explanation: HotStuff (Yin et al. 2019) achieves O(N) message complexity via threshold sigs + leader-driven broadcasts. Pipelined 3-chain commit + optimistic responsiveness + simple view-change. Foundation of Diem/Aptos BFT + modern BFT blockchains.

slides.workedSolution: HotStuff: O(N) per view via threshold sigs; pipelined 3-chain commit; optimistic responsiveness; simple view-change. Foundation of Diem, Aptos, modern BFT chains.

question.question: A Cloudflare Workers function exhibits sub-millisecond cold starts; an equivalent AWS Lambda function has hundreds of ms. Why the gap?
options: Workers use **V8 isolates** (the same as Chrome tabs) — milliseconds to spin up + share a single process; tradeoff is JavaScript/WASM-only + isolation by V8's sandbox. Lambda boots a **Firecracker microVM** (or container) per concurrent invocation — sub-second but still much slower; tradeoff is full language support + strong isolation. WASM at the edge (Workers, Fastly Compute@Edge) merges the two: portable, fast cold-start, strong sandbox.
question.explanation: V8 isolates (Cloudflare Workers) start in <1 ms because they reuse a running V8 process; isolation comes from V8's per-isolate memory + capability boundaries. Firecracker microVMs (Lambda, Fargate) provide stronger OS-level isolation but pay ~100-200 ms cold start for kernel + runtime init (mitigated by SnapStart). WASM is the convergence — sub-ms start with strong sandbox + portable across runtimes (Wasmtime, Wasmer, WasmEdge). The tradeoff is language support: V8 limits to JS/WASM; microVMs run any language.

slides.workedSolution: Workers = V8 isolates (sub-ms, JS/WASM only). Lambda = Firecracker microVMs (~100s ms, any language). WASM converges both: fast + portable + sandboxed.

question.question: How many honest replicas must vote 'commit' in PBFT (N total, f Byzantine) for safety?
question.explanation: PBFT (Castro-Liskov 1999) requires **2f+1** matching commits to commit a request. With N=3f+1 total, 2f+1 is a majority of honest replicas (since at most f are Byzantine, 2f+1 contains at least f+1 honest). Any two such quorums intersect in at least one honest replica, preserving safety. Same quorum size used in prepare phase. View-change collects 2f+1 view-change messages. HotStuff (Yin 2019) preserves the 2f+1 quorum while pipelining 3 phases into a 3-chain commit. Lamport-Shostak-Pease's 3f+1 + the 2f+1 quorum are the central numbers of BFT.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, contrast Nakamoto consensus with classical BFT + sketch the modern blockchain landscape.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Nakamoto consensus** (Bitcoin 2008 Satoshi Nakamoto; Dwork-Naor 1992 PoW; Garay-Kiayias-Leonardos 2015 backbone analysis): permissionless; longest-chain rule; probabilistic finality; selfish mining (Eyal-Sirer 2014); 51% attacks; energy-intensive. **Classical BFT** (Lamport-Shostak-Pease 1982; PBFT Castro-Liskov 1999; HotStuff Yin et al. 2019): permissioned or stake-weighted; 3f+1 quorum; 2f+1 votes; deterministic finality; high throughput but limited validator count. **Modern blockchains** blend: Ethereum 2.0 (PoS via Casper + LMD-GHOST), Cosmos (Tendermint), Aptos + Sui (Move + HotStuff/DAG variants), Solana (Tower BFT + PoH), Algorand (VRF committee), Avalanche (metastable). Buterin's trilemma (security/decentralization/scalability) drives scaling via rollups (Optimism, Arbitrum, zkSync, Starknet) + data-availability layers (Celestia, EigenDA). MEV (Daian 2019 'Flash Boys 2.0') reshaped economics. Modern cloud + service mesh + WASM edge build the application layer on this consensus substrate — the full distributed-systems lineage from Lamport 1978 to 2026.
